full_judgment:
"7. Execution of decisions and orders of a Tribunal. - A Tribunal shall, for the purpose of execution of its decisions and orders, follow, as far as practicable, the provisions of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908 (IV of 1908), relating to the execution of a decree." 

 21. How an Administrative Tribunal will execute its own decisions and orders, is very much a matter within the exclusive and unencroachable jurisdiction of the Administrative Tribunal itself. It is the Administrative Tribunal which is the sole arbiter of the method and procedure with regard to the execution of its own decisions and orders. Rule 7 enjoins upon the Tribunal to-follow. as far as practicable, the provisions of the Code of Civil Procedure, relating to the-execution of a decree. A decision and order directing payment of money to an applicant may thus be enforced by following the provisions of the Code of Civil Procedure relating to the execution of a decree. But the rule-making authority was fully aware that there may be a variety of decisions and orders of the Tribunal which may not by capable of being enforced by following the provisions of the Code of Civil Procedure relating to execution of decree. Rule 7 docs not say that the Tribunal is barred from following any other procedure. It will follow the provisions of the Code of Civil Procedure relating to the execution of a decree "as far as practicable", but as and when it is not practicable to do so, the Tribunal is not powerless. It will not be a lame duck. Its decisions and orders are not meant to be meaningless decorative art pieces. Section 8 of the Act says that its decisions and orders are "binding on the parties". This is not a mere pious legislative wish. The Administrative Tribunal has the fullest jurisdiction to devise its own method and procedure to execute its own decisions and orders, when the provisions of the Code of Civil Procedure cannot be followed. In the present case, for example, it can pass an order in execution (based upon the judgment) giving the respondents a certain period within which to prepare the Gradation List and submit the same to the Tribunal. In this way, no decision or order of the Tribunal will remain inexecutable. The Administrative Tribunal is functioning under a Constitutional mandate and the legislation has armed it to the teeth to be an effective body. This Court, exercising its jurisdiction under Article 102, will not tell the Tribunal in each case whether the provisions of the Code of Civil Procedure are applicable or not. The Tribunal will take that decision itself. If it is wrong in its decision, the Administrative Appellate Tribunal will correct it, for an appeal lies against "any order or decision of an Administrative Tribunal." All questions and problems relating to execution will have to be answered and resolved by the Administrative Tribunal or the Administrative Appellate Tribunal within the periphery of the Act and the Rules.
